Q.	The Latin word X is an adjective derived from a word meaning guest or host. It originally referred to anything connected with care for travelers, pilgrims, and the sick. English borrowed this word three separate times, and the "s" in the middle of the original word is a perfect linguistic timestamp. In Old French, the "s" before the "t" was still pronounced. By around the 17th century, that "s" had gone silent in spoken French. Eventually, in Modern French spelling, the silent "s" was dropped entirely and replaced with a circumflex over the preceding vowel — a written ghost of the lost consonant. The first borrowing came directly from Latin, kept both the "s" and the original meaning of caring for people in need, and gives us Y, the institution where the sick are treated. The second borrowing came through Old French, with the "s" still pronounced — this gives us Z, a cheap travelers' lodging often used by backpackers. The third borrowing came from Modern French (s gone, circumflex in its place), giving us W, an upscale travelers' lodging. A linguistic fossil: the W-Dieu, founded in 651 CE in Paris and still operating today, is actually a Y. The name preserves a memory of the time when all three words W, Y, and Z meant the same thing in Paris.
